### /run-brief: a commit takes only its own files, a run stops at a boundary, the foundation's report reaches each stream's inbox, and a summary says where the time went

[`574a3e6198dc`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/574a3e6198dc0e906c5bc5c7fae696ec38e2d347) · [log `ff8c349b1a7c`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/ff8c349b1a7cd7783917560332df5ed502db827588231a735dfbcdc07b8ca76a.jsonl.gz)

Four additions the user chose before the first run of a brief through its watcher. (1) sync.py commit --only PATH ... commits the named files and folders alone: every other file changed in the working copy is set aside in a change below, and put back uncommitted after the commit, so the files on disk never change. The result collector commits with the paths pipeline.py commit-paths names (verification/, the examples table, the outputs it applied), and the loops' instruction names --only in place of a procedure to follow by hand; on 2026-11-16 a commit of results took a watcher's unfinished merge with it. A collector in a workspace of its own was the plan's wording and is not what this does: every reader of results reads them on the default line, so its commits would have to be landed there one by one, which brings the shared working copy back. (2) brief_run.py stop NAME stops a run at a boundary: run-streams.sh gives each loop a directory for command lines, each running loop is told to end after its cycle, a loop waiting on jobs stops waiting, nothing is run again and the merge is not started; start continues, and stop --now interrupts as before. (3) Landing the foundation puts its closing report into each stream's inbox as an item of a new kind, foundation, which the stream acknowledges. (4) run-streams.sh logs each change of a loop's phase with its time, and a summary says per loop how long it worked, waited on jobs, was blocked, and sat finished while another stream still ran.

Verified by test_commit_only.py on a real jj repository (the named paths committed, a modified, an added and a nested file of another session left uncommitted with their contents), test_brief_run.py (28 tests: a run stopped while a stream waits on jobs, then continued to its merge; the hand-off sent once; the time lines), and test_costs.py run --changed, 26 of 27 files, the one failure an assertion of mine on the order two parallel streams start in, since fixed and run three times. Telling a real loop to end after its cycle is the command path the proof loop's watcher already uses, and is not exercised here with a real session. The working copy went stale during this work and was restored from a backup, compared against jj's own snapshot.

### The default test run runs inline again, never as a verification job, and a passed run is recorded for the push and release gates

[`1ba6d2ed715c`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/1ba6d2ed715c2904ed95251654c87de604d76406) · [log `4cea52ec32b4`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/4cea52ec32b474e38d481508fb9fd1cab080db066f03c25be70249bb4da9e228.jsonl.gz)

The user decided to take the default run out of the verification pipeline: as a job it overlapped other runs in one cargo target directory (VF-034), was cut off with its runner at the Bash tool's 10-minute limit, and skipped the one-at-a-time lock when queued from a line that predated it. verification/default_tests.py (queue, step, supersede, bisect, the unread-file list, flaky counts) and its tests are removed, with verification/default-tests-unread.txt and the watcher's default-tests event.

New lib/tools/default_run.py: a whole default run (test_costs.py run) that passes records the git tree it tested, as jj snapshots the working copy, and only when no file changed during the run, in ~/.cache/in-the-loop/default-runs.jsonl. The record covers a commit of the same tree, or one differing only in traces, decisions and job records. sync.py push and release.py cut ask default_run.py gate --run, which runs the default run inline when no record covers @-; --skip-tests stays the user's alone. Every test_costs.py run holds a lock in the workspace's cargo target directory, so two runs in one workspace take turns.

Docs follow: CLAUDE.md (Verification jobs exempts the default run; Tests says inline, the record and the gate; the tests: queued brief bullet is gone), runtime.md (merges run the default run inline, the watcher's default-tests row and the release gate), the prove-java-change skill, verification/README.md, lib/README.md, llm-dlc/README.md, brief-template.md (one inline test rule replaces the Inline/Queued policy, which also settles the mismatch left by the run-brief merge), validate_example.py's docstring, and a line in VF-034.

[`4160a561f031`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4160a561f0319a201cf73551e77a56177a339f5e) · [log `da5a0a03ac92`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/da5a0a03ac92bb24cbe31f40b395cf3621e86910e7549ee7afce8fea0c0f8baa.jsonl.gz)

At the user's word after the first /run-brief rehearsal (2026-11-17), whose merge loop took the finished streams for empty because their notes were not in its working copy's files, and in which a finished stream waited for the slowest. run-streams.sh now puts each finished stream, done or left blocked, to the watcher at once (conductor.py's new merge question, RUN_STREAMS_MERGE_WAIT, 30 min), while the others still run, and no longer runs the brief's own loop after the streams; a brief without streams still runs as its own loop, now labelled brief. brief_run.py merge BRIEF STREAM merges the stream's @- into the default line as land does, takes its session logs (land now runs sync.py adopt-logs too) and inbox acknowledgements, answers the question merged, records the merge in the brief's Progress (status done once every stream is merged and done, blocked: stream S: ... when one was left blocked) and commits it with the decision; it commits the run's own decision record first, so the watcher's earlier answers don't block it, and run again after a hand-made merge it only records it. Without a watcher nothing is merged and the run's end names the command. conductor.py numbers events under a lock: two streams finishing in the same second both took event 1 and each other's verdict. The skill, llm-dlc/README.md, the brief template, stream-conductor.md's Design 5 and the rehearsal brief (no index.md any more, fresh session ids) say so. Verified with test_costs.py run --changed: 8 test files, 194 tests, all passed, among them new end-to-end tests in test_brief_run.py (both streams merged by the watcher as they finish, the brief done, nothing uncommitted, a second merge recording nothing; a blocked stream merged and named in the status; no watcher, no merge) and a test in test_conductor.py that fails without the lock.

### The watcher of a brief's run collects and commits verification results itself, and landing drops trace output left uncommitted

[`f5d19330ec3f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/f5d19330ec3f13b22638743e997de08e7ef88c09) · [log `da5a0a03ac92`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/da5a0a03ac92bb24cbe31f40b395cf3621e86910e7549ee7afce8fea0c0f8baa.jsonl.gz)

With a watcher, run-streams.sh starts no verification loop. At each look at the queue, brief_run.py wait collects the results that are back and commits them with --only the paths pipeline.py commit-paths names, starts the runner (pipeline.py run, no model) when jobs wait and none is at work, and records the inbox items the streams' committed Progress acknowledges. It returns a 'results' event with the jobs to triage in 'attention'; the watcher triages them as the run-verification skill says. brief_run.py collect does the same by hand, for the report. A verification loop already running keeps the queue as before. Merges and collections take turns by a lock, so the watcher is the one session committing in the default working copy while a run is under way.

land (and so merge) now treats uncommitted trace output (llm-dlc/traces/, llm-dlc/index.json, the decision views, and llm-dlc/README.md when only its session table changed) as nobody's work: it is dropped, not waited for and not carried onto the other line, and the next sync.py run writes it again. In the rehearsal it was there after the foundation landed, and a second real-time merge would have waited for a commit no session was going to make. A move forward that makes another session's uncommitted files conflict is taken back; the jj steps hold sync.py's repository lock; the precise list of generated paths replaces the 'llm-dlc/ or README.md' prefix that sent any file under llm-dlc/ written during a merge into the merge commit.

### A proof by induction and a lemma's summary no longer stand in for a call that writes, throws, or reads what a caller can change

change `qkqpsmqkswql` · [log `485da70bcb76`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/485da70bcb765170eb169d2834f50fdf1093d602f220c87e50df7d8c472f72e1.jsonl.gz)

Three false proofs, each reproduced first on the checker as it was (lib/tests/fixtures/claims/claims/Effects.java, whose main prints what a JVM says): (1) prove --decreases on a method that counts its calls in a static field proved 'result == 1' where a JVM returns 2, because the induction hypothesis replaced the inner call and dropped its write; (2) with a throws clause, the hypothesis returned a value for an inner call the property itself says throws, and proved 'result == n' of a method that never returns; (3) a lemma about a getter, proved in the fresh state where its static field is 0, was used as a summary after the caller wrote the field, and proved 'result == 0' of a method that returns what it wrote. The same held through a callee, through an array a static field holds, for the default locale, and for a lemma whose own assertion reads a field.

Now: a method proved by induction is held to the write checks a summary's method already had (Options::own_induction says the proof is by induction alone, where reads are sound because the inner calls are made in the state of the call under proof); the hypothesis does not cover arguments on which a throws clause says the call throws (the induction then does not go through); a lemma's method, and the lemma's assumption and assertion, may read no static field that is not final, no non-final field or cell of an object that was there before the call, and not the default locale (Engine::reads); a summary is not used while its method's class is still being initialized. A lemma about a method of no parameters now compiles (its assertion is over the result alone).

Which existing results rest on these mechanisms: none uses prove --decreases directly; examples 286 and 288 use lemmas about PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatch(String,String), whose bytecode in the pinned 5.3.19 JAR reads no field and no array (javap), so their results did not rest on the hole; that the tightened checks still prove those lemmas is for a job to confirm. Verified by lib/tests/claims.rs (18 passed, among them the three new tests and the changed lemma test: a method that counts with calls++ is now refused at its read, one that only writes at its write), the summary unit tests, and test_costs.py run --changed (8 of 8 passed: cargo test's 33 binaries and three Python files).

### A preservation proof is non-vacuous only with a witness outside the allowed change, and accept.py asks the outcome to say so

change `ymzlyksqouqq` · [log `30a05ef3c829`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/30a05ef3c829108103c1018da7dce1ad7cbdd94d96d460706bd7d8bae5e7c31f.jsonl.gz)

Step 4 of the evidence stream's brief. A regression check made as a property of the pair of versions (lib/src/pairing.rs, the route of examples 289's and 290's preservation) proves RegressionPair.agree, which returns true on an input inside the allowed change without calling either version. The property check's vacuity probe asked only for an input of the assumption, so it called a proof non-vacuous even when every assumed input lay inside the change. The control: example 289's preservation through its own driver, with only --unchanged-unless replaced by true, was verified and non-vacuous (a capped 5 s probe). 290's recorded witness, servlets=[], lies inside its own allowed change.

The fix: a verified pair with an allowed change is checked once more, meantToChange against result over the same assumption, domain and class path. A proof makes the statement vacuous; a witness, replayed as any is, becomes the statement's, with the new stated.vacuity.outside naming the change. The regression harness's own probe sets outside too, since that harness returns before the probe on an input in the scope. Now the true control is vacuous, 289 with its own change is non-vacuous at servletPath="" (0.3 s more) and 290 at servlets=[0] (capped probes, recorded in both examples' notes). accept.py refuses an establishment of a task with an allowed change whose outcome does not say its witness lies outside that change (unbound) or names another (fail). So 289's and 290's accepted preservation answers are refused until a rerun on a checker with this fix; the other six stay accepted.

Verified: lib/tests/pairing.rs a_pairs_proof_is_vacuous_when_the_allowed_change_covers_every_assumed_input (tool tier, fails without the fix with NonVacuous), three new cases in examples/tools/test_accept.py, the 289 checkout test now expecting preservation refused for this reason; test_costs.py run --changed 8 of 8, estimate, tag and lint clean; validate_example.py 289 and 290 pass. lib/README.md describes the check.

The brief's 'Where it stands' paragraph is out of date: 289's and 290's preservation are refused now, and every accepted answer of 289 and 290 carries no limit about unrecorded artifacts.

> I like chaining the sessions because future sessions learn implicitly from previous sessions -- this is by design. I think auto compaction is probably the way to go. Can this be updated while the current loop is running so as not to disrupt it?

**Reply:**

No, the running loop can't pick up the change. Its bash parsed the whole cycle loop when it started, so nothing written to the script now reaches it. But you can apply the change at a cycle boundary without losing anything. I've made the change and committed it in the side workspace `moonshot`, where it can't touch the loop's working copy.

## The change (`uzporttn`)
- **600k limit:** every moonshot turn passes `--autocompact 600k`. Briefs are left alone because they have their own stopping rules. `FEATURE_LOOP_AUTOCOMPACT` overrides the value; claude accepts 100k to 1M.
- **Compaction with no commit stops the loop:**
  - The loop watches the instruction turn for an automatic compaction. If no commit has landed since the cycle began, or since the previous compaction, it ends the turn right there, which is between model calls, and stops claude's child processes too.
  - It then writes "Stopped …: cycle N (item X) compacted with no commit at T tokens; session … needs attention" to the run record and exits.
- **Unchanged:** sessions stay chained across cycles, and the moonshot prompt gets nothing added. Manual `/compact` turns and the end-of-run summary turn aren't watched.
- **Stats:** `loop_stats.py` counts this as a new stop reason, "compacted, no commit".

**How I tested it:** I put a stand-in `claude` on PATH that emits a compaction event.
- Auto compaction with no commit: the turn ended immediately, no child process was left behind, and the stop reason was written.

**What the brief now says:**
- **The problem:** a moonshot has no acceptance criteria. Sessions stay chained by design, the one-line input gets nothing added, and leaving an item unfinished is fine if the work was productive, since a later pass can return to it.
- **The judgment:** at each automatic compaction, a separate session outside the moonshot loop decides whether the work is hard but still going well, or stuck and needing a person. It reads the transcript, the commits and diff, test runs, jobs, and whether the same failure keeps coming back. Keeping it outside means the moonshot isn't distracted, which fits the conductor's purpose.
- **The actions:** by default it lets the turn go on. If the session is stuck, it stops the loop and queues a decision for you saying why. The brief leaves other actions for the implementer to propose, such as ending the item at its last good commit. Every judgment goes into the decision record with its reasoning.
- **The fallback:** the mechanical stop in `uzporttn` (600k limit, stop on a compaction with no commit) applies when the conductor isn't running or can't decide. The brief notes that `show_progress` already sees the compaction event and holds claude's process id, so that's where the hand-off goes.

> Should we relax the 1GB memory limit? This can easily go to 4GB (or higher), especially as real world changes can be much more complex

**Reply:**

Yes, I'd relax it, but for one-off probes only, and with a hard cap. Some background first.

**Where the 1 GB comes from:** it isn't a limit in the checker. It's the line in `CLAUDE.md:20` (repeated in `verification/README.md:57`) between what an agent may run during its turn and what it must queue as a verification job. The checker itself can already use much more as a job. The trouble is that the agent's quick probes must stay under 1 GB, so it ends up tuning memory to pass that line before it knows whether the real proof works. That's what happened at 03:12–03:16.

To be fair, the two fixes it made there would matter at any limit: 32k fresh variables for every store into an unknown array, and dense per-path models. Real changes would hit both. But the next round of that kind of tuning would mostly be work to satisfy the rule.

**What I'd change:**
1. **Agent probes:** a single inline run of the checker may use up to **4 GB and a few minutes**, inside a `systemd-run` scope with `MemoryMax=4G`. The agent already runs its probes in such scopes, so the cap is easy to enforce. During 286 one of them was killed for running out of memory at its 2 GiB cap, and the loop carried on unharmed.
2. **Tool-tier tests stay at 1 GB.** The default run starts many tests at once, so 4 GB each would overrun the loop's memory. Real-world-sized proofs stay as jobs, as now.
3. **Jobs** need no change. They already declare their memory, and the runner has 80G while one loop runs.

### 40. 2026-11-16 17:08 UTC

> Run the push python command, then I'll invoke the skill. Also give me a quick summary of what "unattended" and "record-as" flags do.

**Reply:**

Everything is pushed and published. `main` and `origin/main` both point at `nvsxqxwk` ("Record session traces"), so no commit on the default line is left behind. The push's check reported 0 errors and 0 warnings, and it uploaded the outstanding session traces. The working copy is empty, so the skill can start.

**`--unattended`** tells the skill you're away for the whole run. It's meant for runs over examples named by number.
- The skill doesn't wait for your approval of each example's claims. It still prints them, checks each against the example's summary and advisory, and accepts them for you when they say no more than the catalog entry does.
- Each claim it accepts this way is recorded as a decision flagged for your later review.
- An example whose claims it isn't sure of is left out of the run and named in the final report, waiting for you.
- Anything else it can decide itself, it decides and records instead of asking. Anything that only you can decide still waits for you, and the rest of the run carries on around it.

**`--record-as NAME`** files the run under an existing loop's name, so its run record and statistics continue that loop's list. With `--record-as prove-examples`, 288 onwards adds to the same record and statistics as 285–287 instead of starting a new loop name.

The command to start the run:
```
/prove-java-change --unattended --record-as prove-examples continue session a4ac2b6c-a5b9-4507-a21e-1b56ae8b2c31: 288 289 290
```

| | prove-examples (285–287) | this run so far (288–290) |

| Context while waiting | median 310k, max 453k | median 352k, max 364k |
| Context while working | median 257k, p90 414k | median 272k, p90 519k |

**Why waiting is so cheap**
- **Proof jobs don't wait in the session.** When the loop leaves an example to wait on its jobs, no Fable tokens are spent. The session only waits while a cycle is still running.
- **What it does wait on is mostly the inline default test run.** The most common waiting calls are polls of that run's log, then checks of the verification queue. Queuing the default run as a job, as I recommended earlier, would remove most of that $8.
- **No cache rebuilds.** No call wrote more than 100k tokens back into the cache. Gaps never let the cache expire, so a wait costs one small poll, not a full context rewrite.

### 76. 2026-11-16 22:32 UTC

> Let the loop use its judgment for now and we will continue to feed the results of this session into fast follow changes. Let's explore how we can alleviate some of the pain of default test runs taking so long, as it's becoming a real bottleneck: I suggest we still queue them as a job on each merge, but that this job should never block the next action. **Reply:**

I agree: run the full suite as a non-blocking job on every merge, and make publishing the only point that waits for a clean result. Here's how I'd build it, with a few more ideas in the same spirit. I'll leave the loop to its own judgment.

### The core design

1. **Queue the default run as a pipeline job, tied to a commit.**
   - Every merge, and every example's last commit, queues `default tests at <change>`, a job that runs `test_costs.py run` and nothing else.
   - It runs in a throwaway jj workspace checked out at that commit, not in the live working copy. The result then belongs to that exact revision, and the loop's ongoing edits can't change what is tested halfway through.
   - Low priority (`nice`, a few CPUs), so it doesn't slow the proof jobs, which matter more.
2. **Nothing waits for it.** The session or watcher that queued it carries on. Its result comes back like any other job, through `wait`.
3. **The watcher triages failures:**
   - **Small and mechanical** (a test-inventory or lint row, a stale index, a doc count): the watcher fixes it in the side workspace, and the fix is merged at the next boundary between examples. The proving session never sees it.
   - **In the area the loop is working on** (the engine, the example's tools): the watcher writes a short note next to `expert-review.md`, for example `test-findings.md`, naming the failing test, the commit, and the commits since the last pass. The next cycle can read it.
   - **Anything else** goes to you.

*… (shortened; the log has the full text)*

**What's built:**
- **Queuing:** `python3 verification/default_tests.py queue [--rev REV] [--why TEXT]` writes a job that runs the default test run on a clean export of that commit. It runs at low priority and keeps its compiled Rust build between runs. The job file can be committed from any workspace, and nothing waits for it.
- **Only the newest runs:** if a newer default-run job is waiting or running when one starts, it exits within seconds and its log says `default tests: superseded by ID`.
- **The watcher triages results:** `watch.py wait` reports each run that comes in, with its commit and the files that failed. Small mechanical failures I fix in the side workspace. Failures in the loop's own area go into a `test-findings.md` file the next cycle can read. Anything else comes to you.
- **The push gate:** `sync.py push` now refuses unless a passed run covers the commit being pushed. That's a run at the same commit, or at an earlier one whose only differences are files no test reads: traces, decisions, job results. `--skip-tests REASON` is there for you to override it.

## What "accepting the claims" decided

Each example has two claims, written by the setup session before any proof is attempted, then frozen:

- **A security claim:** the property the CVE fix is meant to make true. It should hold on the fixed release and fail on the vulnerable release and on a mutant (a deliberately broken copy of the fix).
- **A preservation claim:** outside an "allowed change" region, the two releases behave the same. This catches a "fix" that is secure only because it breaks everything, such as a matcher that denies every request.

The question put to you, and answered by me under `--unattended`, was: "does the loop spend its hours proving *these* claims as stated?" The options and their costs:

| Option | What happens | Cost if wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **Accept** | The loop proves the claims as written | If you meant a different claim: a new setup session restates it, and the proofs are redone. Results on the old claim stay valid but answer a question you didn't ask. |
| **Hold** | The example sits out the run until you read the claims | One run's progress on that example, and nothing else |

The watcher now merges each stream into the default line the moment it finishes, and the merge loop is gone. The rehearsal commits are gone from the line. The full default test run passed on the result: 52 of 52 test files. Nothing is pushed.

**How a run works now**
- When a stream finishes (done, or left blocked), `run-streams.sh` asks the watcher to merge it right away, while the other streams keep running. If nobody answers within 30 minutes, the stream stays unmerged.
- The watcher answers by running `brief_run.py merge BRIEF STREAM`, which:
  - merges the stream's commits into the default line;
  - copies over its session logs;
  - closes the inbox items it acknowledged;
  - answers the question and records the merge in the main brief's Progress;
  - commits all of it.

  The brief's status becomes `done` once every stream is merged and done. If one was left blocked, the status says `blocked: stream S: …`.
- **Conflicts:** a merge that conflicts in real work is taken back. The skill tells the watcher to resolve small, clear conflicts by hand, as the `/prove` watcher does between examples, and otherwise answer `leave` and tell you.
- **After a merge:** the watcher runs the default test run, unless the brief rules tests out. It reports a failure to you rather than fixing it.
- **Without a watcher** nothing is merged, and the end of the run prints the command for each stream.

## The `land` gap

`land` brings the foundation's commits onto the default line, and `merge` now does the same for each stream. It takes one of two paths:

- **Moved forward**, when the line hasn't moved since the workspace was made. It rebases the default working copy onto the workspace's tip.
- **Merged**, when the line has moved. It makes a merge commit, regenerates the trace files and commits.

**Reply:**

I read Codex's 307 answer from its session log, so I have it too. The main points:
- **Approach:** prove the two conversions agree first, then treat the unchanged bcrypt code as one function, using the same checked mechanism Codex suggested for 287's `crypt_raw`. That needs a footprint covering every table bcrypt reads and evidence that nothing writes to them. Loosening `Engine::reads` would be a bypass, not a rule.
- **The claim's JDK citation is wrong:** `getBytes(String)` leaves the handling of unencodable input unspecified; only `getBytes(Charset)` promises replacement. Equivalence has to rest on the pinned JDK 21/25 implementation. `"UTF8"` is a valid alias, so it belongs in a positive control rather than a wrong conversion.
- **Cost is better than feared:** there is no costly `$2a$10$` salt in the frozen domain, because that salt is deliberately short and throws before hashing. Valid salts are cost 5 or 6, at most 64 rounds.
- **I008 (yours):** Codex recommends a new companion claim run under a non-UTF-8 default charset, with the frozen claim kept and its limits recorded. Whether to add it is still your call.

The specialist will come to me directly with questions or results, and I'll pass its packet to preservation as one inbox item when it's done. I'm still watching the run.

I recorded your I008 answer (defer to after the run) as D028. It goes to preservation with the 307 packet, so it records the limit and spends nothing on a companion claim.

On the citation, here are the tradeoffs.

**What's actually wrong.** The assumption's text is: "Both revisions run on the same JDK, whose `getBytes(String)` and `getBytes(Charset)` for UTF-8 encode alike, malformed input and all: both are specified to 'always replace…'".
- The first clause is the premise, and it's true on the pinned OpenJDK 21/25. Both overloads reach the same `encode`, and the replay checks it on both JDKs.
- The second clause is the justification, and it's false for `getBytes(String)`. Its spec leaves unencodable input unspecified.
- So the error is in why the premise is harmless, not in what the proof assumes or what it claims.

**Strictly speaking, restating (#2) is cleaner.** A frozen claim is a published artifact, and this one carries a false sentence about the JDK spec. Read literally, a result would seem to hold on any conforming JDK, which overclaims. Restating would cost:
- a new freeze from you;
- a new hash, so evidence bound to the old one stops counting: the replays, the receipts, and anything `accept.py` checks against the claim. Those would have to be redone before preservation can use them;
- and it changes nothing about what gets proved.

**A finding plus proceeding (#1) is sound.** It corrects the record without touching the hash:
